title: The Shop That Let Customers Wait Outside
passage:
A small bakery in the center of town became famous for one kind of cream bread. On Saturday mornings, a line often formed before opening. The shop was pleased by the demand, but neighbors complained that customers blocked the narrow sidewalk. The bakery tried putting rope barriers along the wall, yet the line still stretched past two doorways when the weather was good.

The owner first considered limiting the number of loaves sold to each customer. That might shorten the line, but it would not solve the main problem. Many people arrived at the same time because they believed the bread would sell out quickly. Even if each person bought less, the crowd could still form.

A staff member suggested numbered tickets. Customers could take a ticket and return later, but the owner worried that people might miss their turn. The bakery had no app and did not want to collect phone numbers. Instead, they created time-window tickets. A ticket might say, ‘Please return between 10:20 and 10:35.’ Each window allowed a limited number of customers. People could spend the waiting time elsewhere and knew they did not need to stay in line.

The first Saturday exposed a weakness. Some customers arrived much earlier than their window because they were afraid the shop would run out. The bakery therefore guaranteed that ticket holders would receive their reserved quantity if they returned during the printed period. This reduced the reason to wait nearby.

Another issue involved visitors who came from far away and did not want to wait an hour. The shop kept a small number of loaves for ordinary walk-in sales, while most of the popular bread used the ticket system. This meant the method did not become an all-or-nothing rule.

After six weeks, sidewalk crowding decreased sharply. The bakery sold about the same amount of bread, but customers were spread across the morning. Nearby shops reported an unexpected benefit: people holding tickets often entered cafés or bookstores while they waited. Some neighbors who had criticized the bakery said the street felt calmer.

The bakery learned that a line is not only a sign of demand. It is also a result of uncertainty. Customers had been waiting because they did not know whether bread would remain later. Once the shop guaranteed a time and quantity, standing physically in line no longer felt necessary. The solution did not increase production or speed up service. It changed what customers knew about the future. By reducing uncertainty, the bakery improved the street without asking people to be more patient or less interested in its product.
translation:
町の中心にある小さなパン屋は、あるクリームパンで人気になり、土曜の朝には開店前から列ができるようになりました。店にとってはうれしいことでしたが、狭い歩道をふさぐため近所から苦情が出ました。壁沿いにロープを置いても、天気の良い日には列が隣の入口まで伸びました。

一人当たりの購入数を制限する案も出ましたが、問題の中心は別にありました。客は『早く来ないと売り切れる』と思って同じ時間に集まっていたため、購入数を減らしても混雑は残る可能性があります。

そこで時間帯付き整理券を試しました。『10時20分〜35分に戻ってください』のように時間を指定し、その時間に戻れば決められた数量を必ず買えるようにしました。電話番号やアプリは使わず、待っている間はその場を離れられます。

最初は、売り切れを心配して指定時間よりかなり早く戻る人がいました。そこで指定時間内なら確実に受け取れることを明確に保証しました。遠くから来て長く待てない人のために、人気商品すべてを整理券制にはせず、少量は通常販売も残しました。

六週間後、歩道の混雑は大きく減りました。販売量はほぼ同じでしたが、客が午前中に分散しました。さらに整理券を持った人が待ち時間に近くのカフェや本屋へ入るようになり、周辺店舗にも思わぬ効果がありました。

店は、列は単なる人気の証拠ではなく『将来が分からないこと』からも生まれると学びました。客は後で買えるか分からないため、その場に並んでいたのです。時間と数量を保証すると、物理的に列を作る必要がなくなりました。生産量を増やしたわけでも、接客を速くしたわけでもありません。未来について客が持つ情報を変えたことで、混雑を減らせたのです。

title: The School Festival's Reusable Decorations
passage:
Every autumn, classes at Nishioka School decorated hallways for the school festival. Colorful paper arches, signs, stars, and hanging shapes appeared for two days and were then removed. Most decorations were made quickly and thrown away afterward. The art club began wondering whether the school could reduce this waste without making every year's festival look the same.

Their first idea was to save all decorations. That failed immediately. Some paper pieces were torn during removal, and storing large three-dimensional objects required more space than the school had. Teachers also pointed out that students valued designing something new each year. Reuse could not simply mean keeping everything unchanged.

The club changed the question. Instead of asking which finished decorations could be reused, they asked which parts could become materials for future designs. They built a set of lightweight wooden frames in three sizes. Classes could cover the frames with paper, cloth, string, or cardboard to create arches, signs, or display walls. At the end of the festival, the temporary surface materials could be removed while the frames remained.

They also created boxes of reusable clips, hooks, and colored cords. Previously, classes had attached decorations with large amounts of tape. The tape was difficult to remove and often damaged both walls and paper. Clips took longer to plan around, but they allowed materials to be separated and saved.

The first year was imperfect. Some students felt restricted by the standard frame sizes. One class wanted a curved entrance that the rectangular frames could not create. Rather than force all classes to use the system, the club made reuse optional and asked participants to report what was difficult. After the festival, they added two flexible frame pieces and more attachment points.

The second year, almost two thirds of the classes used at least one reusable component. The hallways did not look identical because each class covered and combined the frames differently. Storage space was needed, but the frames stacked flat against one wall of a supply room. The school bought less cardboard and tape, and cleanup was faster.

The art club realized that reuse works best when it preserves creativity rather than replacing it. A finished decoration carries one design, but a reusable structure can support many designs. They had shifted from saving objects to saving useful possibilities. This idea later influenced other events. The music club reused stage platforms with different covers, and the science club stored display stands separately from posters. Sustainability became less about keeping old things exactly as they were and more about designing parts that could return in new forms.
translation:
西岡中学校では毎秋の文化祭で、廊下に紙のアーチや看板、星形の飾りなどを大量に作り、二日後には多くを捨てていました。美術部は、毎年同じ見た目にせず、ごみを減らせないか考えました。

最初は完成した飾りを全部保存しようとしましたが、外すと破れる紙も多く、大型の立体飾りを保管する場所もありません。さらに、毎年新しいものを作ること自体が文化祭の楽しみだという意見もありました。

そこで問いを変え、完成品ではなく『次回の材料になる部分』を残すことにしました。三種類の大きさの軽い木製フレームを作り、紙、布、ひも、段ボールなどをかぶせれば、アーチ、看板、展示壁など様々に使えるようにしました。祭り後は表面だけ外し、骨組みは残します。

再利用できるクリップ、フック、色ひもの箱も用意しました。それまで大量に使っていたテープは壁や紙を傷め、材料を分けて残すのが難しかったからです。

初年度には、決まった枠の大きさが創作を制限すると感じる生徒もいました。曲線の入口を作りたいクラスもありました。そこで使用を強制せず、困った点を集め、次年度には曲げられる部品や取り付け場所を増やしました。

二年目には約三分の二のクラスが何らかの再利用部品を使いましたが、表面や組み合わせが違うため廊下は同じ見た目にはなりませんでした。フレームは平らに重ねて倉庫の壁際へ収納でき、段ボールやテープの購入量も減り、片付けも速くなりました。

美術部は、再利用は創造性をなくすのではなく、創造性を支える形にすると成功しやすいと学びました。完成した飾りは一つのデザインしか持ちませんが、再利用可能な構造は多くのデザインを支えられます。『古い物をそのまま残す』のではなく、『別の形で戻ってこられる部品を設計する』ことが持続可能性につながったのです。

title: The Town That Moved a Crosswalk Twice
passage:
A new supermarket opened beside a busy road, and within weeks residents asked for a crosswalk nearby. The nearest existing crossing was almost two hundred meters away. People were already crossing the road informally near the store entrance, especially in the evening. The city agreed that a safer route was needed.

Engineers first proposed placing the crosswalk directly in front of the supermarket. It seemed logical because that was where most people wanted to go. Before construction, however, they observed traffic for several days. Delivery trucks frequently turned into the same entrance, and cars leaving the parking lot needed a clear view of the road. A crossing there would place pedestrians and turning vehicles in conflict.

The city moved the planned crossing about forty meters east. This location had better visibility and fewer turning vehicles. After the crosswalk opened, officials expected pedestrians to use it. Many did, but a significant number continued crossing near the supermarket entrance. The safer crossing required them to walk east, cross, and then walk back west. The extra distance was small, yet people carrying groceries often chose the direct route.

Rather than simply putting up more warning signs, the city studied the walking paths. On the opposite side of the road was a bus stop west of the supermarket. Many customers were traveling between the bus stop and store, so the eastern crosswalk pulled them away from both destinations. The crossing had been designed around vehicle safety but had not fully considered pedestrian movement.

Engineers searched for another location and found a point slightly west of the supermarket where sight lines were still good and delivery traffic was limited. Moving the crossing would cost money, so some officials argued that people should simply use the existing safe route. Residents responded that a safety feature people routinely avoid is not functioning well, even if it meets technical standards.

The city eventually relocated the crossing and added a short pedestrian fence near the store entrance to guide people toward it. Informal crossing decreased noticeably. The first crosswalk had not been unsafe, but it had been inconvenient enough to compete poorly with the risky shortcut.

The project showed why public design often requires revision after real use begins. Maps and traffic models can identify hazards, but they cannot perfectly predict what people will choose. The first location protected pedestrians from turning trucks. The second protected them while also matching the route between the bus stop and supermarket. Neither safety nor convenience alone was sufficient. The successful design emerged when the city treated observed behavior not as disobedience to be punished, but as information about how the street actually worked.
translation:
交通量の多い道路沿いに新しいスーパーが開店すると、住民から近くに横断歩道を作ってほしいという要望が出ました。既存の横断歩道は約二百メートル離れており、夕方には店の前を直接横断する人が増えていました。

技術者は最初、スーパー正面に横断歩道を置く案を考えました。しかし観察すると、その入口には配送トラックが頻繁に曲がり、駐車場から出る車にも見通しが必要でした。そこに横断歩道を置くと歩行者と右左折車がぶつかる危険があります。

そこで約四十メートル東へ移した場所に設置しました。見通しもよく安全でしたが、開通後も店の前を直接渡る人がかなり残りました。安全な横断歩道を使うには一度東へ歩き、渡ってから西へ戻る必要があり、買い物袋を持つ人にはわずかな遠回りでも避けられました。

市が歩行経路を調べると、道路反対側のバス停はスーパーより西にあり、多くの人が『バス停と店』の間を移動していました。東側の横断歩道は車両安全を考えていましたが、歩行者の目的地同士の関係を十分見ていませんでした。

さらに調べると、店より少し西で、見通しがよく配送車の出入りも少ない場所が見つかりました。移設には費用がかかるため『安全な横断歩道があるのだから使えばよい』という意見もありましたが、住民は『日常的に避けられる安全設備は十分機能していない』と主張しました。

最終的に横断歩道を移し、店前には短い歩行者柵を設けて誘導しました。危険な直接横断は大きく減りました。最初の横断歩道が危険だったのではなく、危険な近道に負けるほど不便だったのです。

この例は、公共設計では実際の利用を見て修正することが重要だと示しています。地図や交通モデルで危険は予測できますが、人が何を選ぶかを完全には予測できません。成功した案は安全性だけでも便利さだけでもなく、両方を実際の移動経路に合わせたものでした。人々の行動を単なる規則違反ではなく、街がどう使われているかを示す情報として扱ったことが改善につながったのです。

title: A Weather App for One Mountain
passage:
A hiking group often climbed Mount Takane, a modest mountain that could be reached by bus from the city. Members checked ordinary weather apps before every trip, yet they were sometimes surprised by fog, strong wind, or sudden temperature changes near the top. The forecast for the city below was usually correct, but conditions on the mountain could be different.

One member, Emi, suggested creating a simple local weather page. The group could not build a professional forecasting system, so she proposed collecting observations instead. A small weather sensor was installed at a mountain hut halfway up the trail. Volunteers at the summit recorded temperature, wind strength, visibility, and cloud conditions whenever they visited.

At first, the page displayed the latest numbers without much explanation. Some hikers treated them as a prediction. If the summit had been clear at eight in the morning, they assumed it would remain clear in the afternoon. Emi realized that current observations and forecasts were being confused. She added time stamps and a clear heading: ‘Recent conditions — not a future forecast.’

The group then compared their observations with official regional forecasts. They found several patterns. Strong northern winds tended to be greater near the summit than in the city, and temperature differences between the base and top were often larger on clear nights. However, the group avoided turning these patterns into precise rules. The data covered only one mountain and only days when volunteers visited. Bad-weather days were actually underrepresented because fewer people climbed then.

To make the page useful without pretending to know too much, they added practical ranges rather than exact predictions. A message might say, ‘Summit conditions can be 5–8°C colder than the bus stop today; carry an extra layer.’ Another reminded users that cloud can reduce visibility rapidly even when the city is sunny. Links to official warnings remained at the top of the page.

After a year, local hikers used the page regularly, especially in spring and autumn. The group received requests to add neighboring mountains, but Emi resisted expanding too quickly. Each location would need its own sensors, volunteers, and careful interpretation. Copying Mount Takane's patterns elsewhere could create false confidence.

The project taught the group a lesson about local data. More specific information can be valuable, but specificity does not automatically make information reliable. Their page was useful because it openly showed what had been measured, when it had been measured, and what remained uncertain. It did not replace official forecasts. Instead, it added local context that helped hikers prepare for conditions the city forecast could not describe in detail.
translation:
登山グループは、市内からバスで行ける高嶺山へよく出かけていました。毎回一般的な天気アプリを確認していましたが、山頂付近で霧、強風、急な気温変化に驚くことがありました。市街地の予報自体は正しくても、山では条件が違うからです。

メンバーのエミは、地域限定の簡単な気象ページを作ることを提案しました。専門的な予報システムは作れないため、途中の山小屋に小型センサーを設置し、山頂へ行ったボランティアが気温、風、視界、雲の状態を記録しました。

最初は最新数値だけを表示したため、利用者がそれを予報だと誤解しました。朝八時に晴れていたから午後も晴れる、と考える人がいたのです。そこで時刻を明示し、『最近の観測—未来の予報ではありません』と表示しました。

公式予報と観測を比較すると、北風の日には山頂の風が市内より強いこと、晴れた夜は麓と山頂の温度差が大きくなることなどの傾向が見えました。ただし、観測は一つの山だけで、しかもボランティアが登った日に偏っています。悪天候の日ほど登山者が少ないため、危険な日のデータが少ないという偏りもありました。

そこで正確な予報のように見せず、『今日は山頂がバス停より5〜8度低くなる可能性があるので上着を』など、準備に役立つ幅を示しました。市内が晴れていても雲で視界が急に悪くなることも知らせ、公式警報へのリンクは常に上部に置きました。

一年後には地域の登山者に利用されるようになりました。他の山への拡張要望もありましたが、エミは急いで広げませんでした。山ごとにセンサーや観測者、解釈が必要で、高嶺山の傾向を他へコピーすると誤った安心感を生むからです。

この活動から、地域に特化した情報は価値がありますが、具体的だからといって自動的に信頼できるわけではないと学びました。役に立ったのは、何をいつ測ったか、そして何が分からないかまで明確に示したからです。公式予報を置き換えるのではなく、公式情報に地域の文脈を加える役割を果たしました。

title: The Library's Noisy Success
passage:
A public library opened a new children's area with bright rugs, picture books, puzzles, and low tables. The goal was to make young children feel welcome. Within weeks, the area became popular. Families stayed longer, weekend attendance increased, and more picture books were borrowed. Yet the library began receiving complaints from adults who used nearby desks for quiet study.

The director faced an uncomfortable situation: the new area was succeeding according to its original goals and failing according to the needs of another group. Some staff suggested stricter noise rules for children. Others argued that expecting very young children to remain silent would defeat the purpose of the space.

The library measured noise at different times and mapped how sound traveled through the building. The problem was strongest near an open staircase that connected the children's floor to the study floor above. Sound rose through the large opening even when children were not shouting. Moving the children's area would be expensive, and closing the staircase was impossible because it was an important emergency route.

An acoustic specialist proposed several smaller changes. Fabric panels were added to one wall, rubber feet were placed under movable chairs, and the noisiest puzzle table was shifted away from the staircase. A row of tall bookshelves created a partial barrier, though fire regulations required open paths. The library also moved some quiet study desks farther from the stair opening.

These changes reduced average noise but did not create silence. The director then added a second type of response: clearer expectations. A sign at the entrance to the study floor explained that some family noise might be heard during daytime hours and pointed to a smaller ‘deep quiet’ room at the back. Meanwhile, staff in the children's area encouraged indoor voices without treating ordinary child conversation as a problem.

Complaints decreased, though they did not disappear. More importantly, users had better choices. People who needed strong quiet could choose the back room, while families could use the children's area without feeling that every sound was unacceptable.

The library learned that shared public spaces often contain goals that cannot be perfectly maximized at the same time. A lively children's program and absolute silence are difficult to place beside each other. The answer was not to declare one group more important. It was to reduce unnecessary noise, separate activities where possible, and make the remaining trade-off visible. The new children's area had not been a mistake. Its popularity simply revealed that successful services can create new problems that deserve design attention of their own.
translation:
公共図書館が、明るい敷物、絵本、パズル、低い机を置いた新しい子どもエリアを作ると、家族の滞在時間や週末利用、絵本の貸出が増えました。ところが近くの机で静かに勉強する大人から騒音への苦情が出ました。

難しかったのは、子どもエリアが本来の目標では成功していることでした。子どもへ厳しい静けさを求めれば、歓迎する空間という目的が失われます。一方、勉強する人の困りごとも無視できません。

音を測り、建物内でどう広がるか調べると、子ども階と上の学習階をつなぐ開放階段から音が上へ伝わっていることが分かりました。子どもエリアを移すのは高額で、階段は避難経路でもあるため閉鎖できません。

そこで壁に布製吸音パネルを付け、椅子脚にゴムを付け、最も音が出るパズル台を階段から遠ざけました。高い本棚で一部を仕切り、静かな学習机の一部も階段から離しました。

平均的な騒音は下がりましたが、完全な静寂にはなりません。そこで学習階には『昼間は家族エリアの音が聞こえることがあります』と案内し、より静かな小部屋を示しました。子ども側では普通の会話まで悪いものとせず、室内の声量を促しました。

苦情は減り、何より利用者が選べるようになりました。強い静けさが必要な人は奥の部屋へ行き、家族はすべての音を責められる感覚なく利用できます。

図書館は、公共空間には同時に最大化できない目標があると学びました。活発な子ども活動と完全な静寂は隣接すると衝突します。一方を優先すると宣言するのではなく、不要な音を減らし、可能な範囲で活動を分け、残るトレードオフを利用者へ明確にすることが必要でした。人気サービスが新しい問題を生むことは、元のサービスが失敗だったという意味ではありません。成功によって次の設計課題が見えることもあるのです。

title: The Recycling Bin with the Wrong Picture
passage:
A station installed new recycling bins with separate openings for plastic bottles, cans, and other waste. The bins looked modern and used large symbols instead of long written instructions. Yet after several weeks, cleaning staff reported that plastic-bottle sections contained many paper cups and food containers. The city assumed travelers were ignoring the rules.

A university design class studied the bins. Students watched from a distance without speaking to users. They noticed that many people looked at the symbols for only a second before choosing an opening. One image intended to represent a plastic bottle showed a simple cylinder with a cap. From several steps away, it also resembled a takeaway drink cup.

The students tested three new labels on temporary cardboard covers. One used a more detailed bottle drawing, one used a photograph, and one combined a drawing with examples of items that did not belong there. They placed the versions at different stations and counted sorting errors for several days.

The photograph performed well when the bin was clean and brightly lit, but glare sometimes made it difficult to see. The detailed drawing also improved results. Surprisingly, the strongest version included both a bottle image and a small crossed-out picture of a paper cup. Apparently, showing a common mistake helped people decide faster than a positive example alone.

The class then interviewed passengers. Most people said they wanted to sort waste correctly but were usually carrying bags, checking train times, or moving with a crowd. They did not stop to read carefully. The label had only a brief moment to communicate. This changed how the city interpreted the problem. What looked like careless behavior was often hurried interpretation.

New labels were installed across the station. Sorting errors decreased, although they did not vanish. Food packaging remained especially confusing because materials varied. The city added a small color strip that matched symbols printed on some station food containers, creating a link between packaging and bins.

The students learned that instructions should be tested under the conditions in which they are actually used. A symbol that seems obvious when examined at a desk may fail when seen from three meters away by someone in a hurry. They also learned that error data can be useful design information. Repeated mistakes are not always evidence that users refuse to follow rules. Sometimes they show that the rule is being communicated poorly. Improving the picture did not change the recycling system itself, but it made the intended choice easier to recognize in the few seconds people were willing to give it.
translation:
駅にペットボトル、缶、その他のごみを分ける新しい回収箱が設置されました。長い説明文の代わりに大きな絵記号を使っていましたが、数週間後、ペットボトル欄に紙コップや食品容器が多く入っていると清掃員から報告されました。市は利用者がルールを無視していると思いました。

大学のデザイン授業で観察すると、多くの人は記号を一秒ほどしか見ずに捨てていました。ペットボトルを表す単純な円筒形の絵が、数メートル離れると持ち帰り用カップにも見えていたのです。

学生は三種類の仮表示を試しました。詳しいボトルの絵、写真、そして正しいボトル絵と『紙コップは不可』を示す×印付きの絵です。複数駅で誤投入を数えると、写真も詳細な絵も改善しましたが、最も効果が高かったのはよくある間違いを×印で示した表示でした。

利用者への聞き取りでは、多くの人が正しく分けたいと思っていても、荷物を持ち、電車時刻を確認し、人の流れの中で急いでいるため、長く読まないことが分かりました。問題は無責任さだけでなく、短時間で判断しなければならない状況にありました。

新しい表示を駅全体へ導入すると誤投入は減りました。ただ食品包装は素材が複雑で迷いやすいため、一部の駅販売容器にも回収箱と同じ色記号を付ける工夫をしました。

学生は、説明は実際に使われる条件で試す必要があると学びました。机の前でじっくり見れば明白な記号でも、三メートル離れ、急いでいる人には伝わらないことがあります。また、繰り返される間違いは利用者の態度だけでなく、説明設計の弱さを示すデータにもなります。回収制度自体を変えず、わずかな表示改善で短い判断時間の中でも正しい選択を見つけやすくできたのです。

title: A Club with No Permanent Leader
passage:
The photography club at Minami High had a problem whenever its president was absent. The president usually chose meeting topics, checked equipment, contacted teachers, and organized exhibitions. Other members were capable, but they waited for instructions because responsibilities had become concentrated in one person. When the president became ill for two weeks, club activities nearly stopped.

At first, members thought the obvious solution was to choose a vice president. That would provide a backup, but a teacher asked whether the same problem might simply move from one person to two. The club decided to experiment with rotating roles instead.

Four roles were defined: meeting facilitator, equipment checker, communication contact, and project recorder. Roles changed every two weeks. Newer members could begin with recorder or equipment duties before trying facilitation. A shared checklist described basic tasks so that each person did not have to invent the role again.

The first month was messy. Some members forgot duties because they were used to the president handling them. Two people sent the same message to a teacher, while no one charged several camera batteries. The club updated the checklist and added a five-minute handover at the end of each rotation. The outgoing member explained what was unfinished and what the next person should watch.

The system also changed meetings. When different students facilitated, the style varied. One student preferred quick decisions, while another asked everyone to speak before choosing a plan. Members sometimes found the differences frustrating, but they also discovered methods they liked. The former president said she had never realized how strongly her personal habits had shaped the club.

By the end of the term, activities no longer stopped when one student was absent. The club still elected a president to represent it officially, but the title carried fewer daily tasks. Leadership had become partly distributed through routines rather than held entirely by one person.

The experiment did not prove that every group should rotate every job. Some tasks require experience, and constant change can be inefficient. What the club learned was to distinguish authority from knowledge. They had once depended on the president not because only she could make decisions, but because important information existed mainly in her memory. Checklists, shared records, and handovers made that knowledge available to others. The strongest improvement was not that everyone became a leader. It was that the group became able to continue functioning when one leader was missing.
translation:
南高校の写真部では、部長が休むと活動が止まりやすい問題がありました。部長が議題決め、機材確認、先生への連絡、展示準備まで多くを担当し、他の部員も能力はあるのに指示を待つ習慣ができていました。部長が二週間病気で休んだとき、活動はほぼ停止しました。

副部長を決めればよいという案が出ましたが、先生は『依存先が一人から二人になるだけではないか』と問いかけました。そこで役割を交代制にしました。

会議進行、機材確認、連絡担当、記録担当の四つを作り、二週間ごとに交代します。新入部員は記録や機材から始め、慣れてから進行役もできます。基本作業は共有チェックリストにまとめました。

最初の一か月は混乱し、同じ先生へ二人が連絡したり、逆にカメラの充電を誰もしなかったりしました。そこでチェックリストを更新し、交代時に五分間の引き継ぎを行い、未完了事項や注意点を次の人へ伝えるようにしました。

会議の雰囲気も変わりました。素早く決める進行役もいれば、全員の発言を聞いてから決める人もいました。違いに戸惑うこともありましたが、部員は様々なやり方を学びました。以前の部長自身も、自分の習慣が部全体の進め方に大きく影響していたことに初めて気づきました。

学期末には、一人が休んでも活動が止まらなくなりました。公式代表として部長は残りましたが、日常業務の多くは共有されました。

この方法がすべての組織に正しいわけではありません。経験が必要な役割もあり、頻繁な交代が非効率な場合もあります。写真部が学んだのは、権限と知識を分けて考えることでした。以前は部長しか判断できなかったのではなく、重要情報が部長の記憶の中に集中していたのです。チェックリスト、共有記録、引き継ぎによって知識を共有し、『全員をリーダーにする』より『一人がいなくても続けられる組織にする』ことが最大の改善でした。

title: The Farm That Measured Shade
passage:
A small vegetable farm installed rows of solar panels above part of its land. The panels were raised high enough for workers and small machines to pass underneath. The farmer, Mr. Ueda, hoped to produce electricity without giving up agricultural use. Some neighbors predicted that vegetables under the panels would grow poorly because of reduced sunlight.

Rather than planting the same crop everywhere, Mr. Ueda treated the first season as an experiment. Lettuce, spinach, tomatoes, and beans were planted both under panels and in full sun. Sensors recorded soil temperature and moisture. Workers measured plant growth every week and kept separate harvest records.

The results were not simple. Tomatoes produced less fruit under the panels, confirming the concern about sunlight. Lettuce, however, performed surprisingly well during the hottest part of summer. Plants in full sun sometimes became stressed during afternoon heat, while shaded lettuce lost less water and remained usable for longer. Spinach showed a similar pattern, though too much shade slowed growth in spring. Beans were less affected than expected.

Water use also changed. Soil beneath the panels dried more slowly, so irrigation could be reduced in midsummer. But rainfall distribution became uneven because water ran off the panel edges. Some narrow strips became wetter than others. The farm adjusted drainage channels and moved irrigation lines rather than assuming the entire shaded area behaved the same.

At the end of the season, a newspaper visited and asked whether solar panels were ‘good or bad for farming.’ Mr. Ueda refused the simple choice. They were bad for some crops in some periods and helpful for others under certain conditions. The economic result also depended on electricity prices, installation costs, and the value of each crop.

In the second year, the farm placed heat-sensitive leafy vegetables in the areas with stronger afternoon shade and kept tomatoes in sunnier rows. Workers also experimented with the distance between panel rows to create different light patterns. The system became less like placing a roof over a field and more like managing several small climates.

The project taught Mr. Ueda the danger of average conditions. Saying that a panel reduced sunlight by a certain percentage did not tell him what happened at noon, in spring, after rain, or to a particular crop. Useful decisions came from measuring how shade changed conditions over time and matching crops to those differences. The solar panels did not produce one universal effect. They created a new set of trade-offs that could be managed only by paying attention to place, season, and plant needs.
translation:
小規模農家の上田さんは、畑の一部に高い位置へ太陽光パネルを並べ、農作業と発電を両立しようとしました。近所からは、日光が減るため野菜が育たないのではないかという心配が出ました。

上田さんは初年度を実験と考え、レタス、ホウレンソウ、トマト、豆をパネル下と日なたの両方へ植えました。土壌温度や水分をセンサーで測り、成長や収穫量を分けて記録しました。

結果は単純ではありませんでした。トマトはパネル下で収量が減り、日光不足の影響が確認されました。一方、レタスは真夏に意外と良く育ちました。日なたでは午後の高温で弱ることがありましたが、日陰では水分を失いにくく、長く商品状態を保てました。ホウレンソウも似ていましたが、春は日陰が強すぎると成長が遅れました。豆は予想ほど影響を受けませんでした。

土が乾きにくいため真夏の水やりは減らせましたが、パネル端から雨水が落ちるため、水が集まる細い帯もできました。排水溝や灌水位置を調整し、パネル下全体を同じ環境とは考えないようにしました。

新聞記者から『太陽光パネルは農業に良いか悪いか』と聞かれた上田さんは、二択では答えられないと話しました。作物や季節によって不利にも有利にもなり、経済性も電気価格、設置費、作物価格で変わります。

二年目には暑さに弱い葉物を午後の日陰が強い場所へ、トマトをより明るい列へ配置しました。パネル間隔も変え、複数の光環境を作りました。畑に屋根を置くというより、小さな気候をいくつも管理する形になったのです。

この経験から、平均値だけでは判断できないと分かりました。『日光が何％減る』という数字だけでは、昼、春、雨後、特定作物で何が起きるかは分かりません。場所、季節、植物の必要に合わせ、時間による変化を測ることで初めて役立つ判断ができます。パネルは一つの普遍的な効果を生むのではなく、管理可能な新しいトレードオフを生んだのです。

title: The Town Hall's One-Page Form
passage:
Residents applying for a child-care support program had to complete a six-page form at the town hall. The form had grown over many years as new legal requirements and administrative checks were added. Staff members believed every question was necessary, yet applicants often left spaces blank or attached the wrong documents. This created extra phone calls and repeat visits.

A new staff member, Ms. Hayashi, suggested reviewing the form from the applicant's point of view. She discovered that several questions asked for information the town already possessed, such as address and household registration details. Some sections were needed only for uncommon cases, but every applicant had to read them. Instructions appeared in small text at the end of the form, far from the questions they explained.

The office could not remove legal requirements, but it could change how information was collected. The main application became one page containing only information most people needed to provide directly. Existing government data was filled in automatically after the applicant gave permission. Less common situations, such as living separately from a registered spouse, triggered an additional page only when relevant.

The office also changed document instructions. Instead of a long list saying which certificates might be necessary, the form asked three simple yes-or-no questions. Based on the answers, staff handed applicants a short personalized checklist. Online applicants received the same checklist automatically.

Some staff worried that the simplified form would hide important details and lead to mistakes. During a two-month trial, every application was checked against the old process. The office found that missing documents decreased and staff spent less time explaining basic steps. A few unusual cases took slightly longer because staff had to open additional forms, but those cases were a small share of applications.

The most surprising change was in conversations at the counter. Staff said they could spend more time discussing actual family circumstances because less time was used correcting boxes and searching for attachments. The form had become shorter, but the service had not become less careful. Attention had shifted from routine data entry to cases that required judgment.

Ms. Hayashi learned that administrative complexity can accumulate quietly. Each added question may have a reasonable purpose, yet the combined result can become difficult for everyone. Simplification did not mean deleting rules. It meant separating information that government already knew, information most people must provide, and information needed only in special cases. By making the common path simple and allowing complexity to appear only when necessary, the town improved both accuracy and user experience.
translation:
子育て支援制度へ申し込む住民は、町役場で六ページの申請書を書く必要がありました。法律上の要件や確認項目が長年追加され、職員はすべて必要だと考えていましたが、空欄や添付書類の間違いが多く、電話確認や再来庁が発生していました。

新任の林さんが申請者の視点で見直すと、住所や住民登録情報など、役場がすでに持つ情報を再度書かせる項目がありました。また、特殊な場合にしか必要でない説明を全員が読まなければならず、説明文も関連する質問から離れた場所に小さく書かれていました。

法律上必要な内容は削除できませんが、集め方は変えられます。主申請書を一ページにし、ほとんどの人が自分で提供する情報だけを残しました。本人の同意があれば既存行政データを自動入力し、別居など特殊な状況だけ追加ページを使う方式にしました。

添付書類も長い一覧ではなく、三つのはい・いいえ質問に答えると、その人に必要な書類だけを短い一覧で示すようにしました。オンライン申請も同じ仕組みにしました。

簡単にしすぎて重要情報を見落とすという心配があり、二か月は旧方式と照合しました。その結果、書類不足は減り、基本説明に使う時間も短くなりました。特殊案件では追加フォームを開くため少し時間が増えましたが、件数は少数でした。

窓口では、職員がチェック欄の修正より家族の実際の事情を聞く時間を増やせたという変化もありました。書類が短くなっても、対応が雑になったわけではありません。定型入力から判断が必要なケースへ注意を移せたのです。

林さんは、行政の複雑さは一つ一つ合理的な追加が積み重なって生まれると学びました。簡略化とは規則を消すことではなく、『行政がすでに知る情報』『大多数が入力する情報』『特殊な場合だけ必要な情報』を分けることです。普通の道を簡単にし、必要なときだけ複雑さを出すことで、正確さと使いやすさを同時に改善できました。

title: The Classroom Temperature Debate
passage:
In early summer, Class 2A argued almost every day about the air conditioner. Students near the windows felt hot in the afternoon sun, while students directly below the air vents complained that they were cold. Someone changed the temperature setting whenever the teacher looked away. By the end of the week, the remote control had become an object of conflict.

The teacher could have set one fixed temperature and forbidden changes. Instead, she asked the class to collect evidence. For three days, students placed simple thermometers at six locations and recorded temperatures every hour. They also marked whether sunlight was reaching each area and asked students to rate how comfortable they felt.

The results showed that one thermostat setting did not create one classroom temperature. At two in the afternoon, the sunny window area could be almost four degrees warmer than the desks near the strongest vent. Comfort ratings also differed even at similar temperatures. Some students preferred cooler air, while others felt cold easily.

The class first tried lowering blinds on the sunny windows. This reduced the temperature difference but also made the room darker. They adjusted only the upper parts of the blinds so natural light could still enter. They then redirected two vent covers slightly upward to reduce direct cold air on students. These small physical changes made the room more even before anyone touched the thermostat.

Next, the class agreed on a temperature range rather than one exact setting. If most readings stayed within the range, the remote would not be changed immediately because one person's discomfort might be caused by location rather than the whole room. Students who still felt cold could keep a light sweater at school, while seating near the hottest windows rotated every two weeks.

The discussion did not eliminate every complaint. On humid days, the same temperature felt warmer, and after physical education some students wanted stronger cooling. The class added a short ventilation period after lunch and accepted that temporary adjustments were sometimes reasonable. The rules became guidelines rather than rigid commands.

By July, arguments about the remote had nearly disappeared. The class had not discovered a perfect temperature. Instead, they had learned that the original debate had been framed too simply. ‘What temperature should the air conditioner be?’ assumed that everyone experienced the same environment. In reality, sunlight, airflow, humidity, clothing, activity, and individual preference all mattered. Once the class addressed the differences in the room, the number on the thermostat became less important. The students learned that disagreements sometimes persist not because people refuse to compromise, but because they are responding honestly to different conditions.
translation:
初夏、2Aではエアコン温度をめぐる口論が毎日のように起きていました。窓側は午後の日差しで暑く、吹き出し口の真下は寒く、先生が見ていない間に誰かが設定温度を変えていました。

先生は一つの温度を固定する代わりに、証拠を集めようと提案しました。六か所に温度計を置き、三日間、一時間ごとの温度、日差しの有無、各自の快適さを記録しました。

結果、同じ設定でも教室内の温度は同じではないと分かりました。午後二時には日なたの窓側が強い吹き出し口付近より四度近く高いことがあり、同じ温度でも暑いと感じる人、寒いと感じる人がいました。

まず日当たりの強い窓のブラインドを下げました。温度差は減りましたが暗くなったため、上側だけ調整して自然光を残しました。さらに二つの吹き出し口を少し上向きにし、直接冷風が当たりにくくしました。設定温度を変える前に物理的な差を小さくしたのです。

次に一つの数字ではなく温度範囲を決めました。多くの場所が範囲内なら、誰か一人が不快でもすぐ設定を変えず、場所の影響を考えます。寒がりの生徒は薄手の上着を置き、暑い窓側の席は二週間ごとに交代しました。

湿度が高い日や体育後など、同じ温度でも状況が違うため、昼休み後に短時間換気し、必要なら一時調整することも認めました。規則は絶対命令ではなく目安になりました。

七月にはリモコンをめぐる争いはほぼなくなりました。完璧な温度を発見したのではありません。『エアコンを何度にするか』という最初の問いが単純すぎたのです。日差し、風、湿度、服装、活動量、個人差があり、人は本当に異なる条件へ反応していました。教室内の差を減らすと、設定数字そのものの重要性が下がりました。対立が続くのは妥協する気がないからではなく、異なる現実を経験しているからという場合もあるのです。
